1:
The word that opens the chapter draws four notes. Clarke gives the Hebrew behind it, Hallelu-Yah, praise ye Jah, which the Greek translators and John after them carried over in Greek letters rather than rendering, and adds that the heathen seem to have borrowed the form, since the paeans to Apollo began and ended with a cry he takes for a corruption of the same words. Robertson counts its occurrences — fifteen Psalms begin or end with it, and in the New Testament it is found only in this chapter, four times — and identifies the Great Hallel as the group sung chiefly at passover and tabernacles. Bede translates it and explains why it is left untranslated: although the words can be rendered, the authority of the original tongue is preserved to them out of reverence for their sacredness. Gill notes that the repetition shows how hearty and constant the praise was. Wesley goes behind the syllable to the name, tracing it from the I will be given to Moses through the is, and was, and is to come of the earlier chapters to the point where the title drops to Jah, he that is — past and future swallowed up in a present where the long-expected coming is no longer awaited.

On the ground of the praise the voices divide between the crime and its punishment. Bede reduces the charge to two counts, that the harlot corrupted herself with the bad and persecuted the good, and holds that these comprehend all the crimes of the wicked. Barnes reads the chapter as an episode delaying the final catastrophe in order to display the effect of Babylon's fall, and lays the whole out in parts. Henry watches what the praise does rather than what it says: their prayers are turned into praises and their hosannas end in halleluias, and when they cried Alleluia her fire burned the fiercer — the surest way to have our deliverances continued being to give God the glory for what he has done, so that praising him for what we have is praying most effectually for what is not yet done. Bede and Robertson converge on the tense from opposite directions: Bede insists that the smoke rises, not will rise, since Babylon is always going into perdition and is in part already burning while Jerusalem passes into paradise; Robertson renders the same verb as keeping on going up, the smoke of the city's ruin standing where incense stood earlier in the book.

Who the four and twenty elders are is not settled. Barnes takes them for representatives of the church, interested in its welfare and now rejoicing in the destruction of its last foe; Gill takes them for the churches and ministers of the several periods; Ellicott divides the two companies, the elders representing the Church and the living beings nature, and corrects the English tense, God who sitteth rather than sat; Clarke alone restricts them to the true Church converted from among the Jews. Wesley notices something none of the others do — that the order of naming has been reversed. Elsewhere the living creatures come first, because praise moves from the centre outward; here, with the judgments fulfilled, it moves back from the circumference to the centre, and so the elders are named first.
5:
The voice out of the throne gets three answers. Barnes reasons that it cannot be God, since the command is praise our God, and hardly the Messiah unless he identifies himself with the church, so it must be a responsive voice from those nearest the throne. Robertson excludes God, the Lamb and the temple and assigns it to an angel of the Presence; Wesley thinks it came from the four living creatures; Clarke reads the summons as levelling every distinction, all giving glory whether redeemed from Jews or Gentiles.

Barnes then draws a distinction in the sound that nobody else notices. In the first verse John heard a great voice he recognised at once as a multitude; here he heard only what resembled one, indistinct, like roaring waters or muttering thunder — a sound both louder and more remote — and reaches for Homer to describe it. Robertson accounts for the same indistinctness grammatically: the participle stands in the genitive plural because the roll of the waters and the roar of the thunders were not articulate, and he identifies this second multitude not with the angels of the first verse but with the redeemed. He also makes the verb of reigning ingressive, God becoming king with the fall of the world power. Clarke reports a textual variant: many manuscripts, most versions, and the two most ancient commentators on the book add our, so the line reads Our Lord God, the Almighty, reigneth — and he draws the consolation that the Almighty never trusts the reins out of his hands. Henry hears a concert: the chorus large and loud, no discord in heaven, no jarring string nor untuned key.

What the marriage means is disputed in time as much as in sense. Henry reports two views, the conversion of the Jews or the general resurrection, and prefers the first; Clarke takes it for a state of Christianity more glorious than any before; Wesley says it is near at hand, and adds that what it implies none of the spirits of just men, even in paradise, yet know. Robertson sets the figure in its history — God the bridegroom of Israel in the prophets, Christ of the kingdom in the apostles — and notes that this book carries three figures of women, the Mother, the Harlot and the Bride. Barnes observes that the propriety of the image comes from the contrast with the meretricious woman just drawn.

The fine linen divides them, and not along the lines the schools would predict. Barnes insists it is given and therefore not the wearer's own: the righteousness obtained by faith through the Redeemer's merits. Clarke denies this in terms: the fine linen is not the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, since the text calls it the righteousness of the saints — what the grace and Spirit of Christ has wrought in them. Henry will have both, Christ's righteousness imputed for justification and imparted for sanctification, the white robe of absolution and adoption together with the white robe of purity; Wesley says the same more briefly. Ellicott notes that the word is plural, righteousnesses, and holds the halves together — the source is divine, since it was given her to be so arrayed, yet it is no fictitious righteousness but really hers. Robertson, rendering it the righteous acts of the saints, draws the consequence that there is work for the Bride as well as for Christ. Ellicott adds that the verse is not part of the song, which closes when the wife is said to have made herself ready, and that the dress answers the harlot's, whose ostentatious colours are tokens of qualities more conspicuous than abiding. Gill tells the reader what byssus is — said to grow on a tree the height of a poplar with leaves like a willow, brought from Judea into Egypt and used there in most holy things.
9:
Who gives the order to write is left open. Gill offers three candidates — the voice from the throne, the angel who had attended John throughout, or the angel who had offered to show him the judgment of the great whore — while Ellicott says the simplest opinion is that it is the angel of the seventeenth chapter, and Robertson allows the same without pressing it. Wesley finds a reason for the command: John was so amazed that he needed reminding to write, and the second saying comes after a little pause. Barnes explains it by the weight of the thing said, which had to be fixed in the mind against the trials to come.

On the beatitude the two most technical voices give different totals. Ellicott calls it one of the six benedictions of the Apocalypse and lists them; Robertson calls it the fourth of seven. Ellicott adds a caution about method: we must not draw too sharp a distinction, as some have done, between the bride and the guests, since the imagery is varied precisely to give force to truths no emblem can express. Robertson enters the same caution from the other side, quoting Swete that apocalyptic symbolism has laws of interpretation of its own by which the student must be guided. Barnes fills in the background, the marriage-supper being a familiar Jewish figure for the happiness of heaven, and Clarke refers it to the parable of the marriage of the king's son.

What John did at the angel's feet, and whether it was wrong, divides them completely. Gill takes it as plain fault: John forgot himself, worship being due to God alone, and the act is not to be excused. Wesley agrees that it was worship and says John mistook the angel for the angel of the covenant, adding that to worship the highest creature is flat idolatry. Clarke contradicts him on both counts: great as the angel was, John could not have mistaken him for Christ or for the Father, and the prostration was not an act of religious worship at all but the reverence any Asiatic would pay a superior — John's real mistake being to think himself under obligation to the angel for the information. Robertson leaves the motive open, John either taking the angel to represent God or being beside himself with excitement, but calls it a temptation to worship an angel. Barnes takes the same view and then fences the inference: there is not the slightest intimation that this was the Messiah, so the passage yields no evidence that it would be improper to worship him, and the only fair conclusion is that religious homage to an angel is wrong. Robertson makes the same point positively, glossing the command worship God as including Christ, who is the Son of God. Ellicott turns the episode into an argument for the book: the immediate checking of the impulse here and again at the end supplies indirect evidence of its genuineness, and gives it a moral tone immeasurably superior to the vision-books of pretended revelations.

The reason the angel gives is read as an argument about rank. Clarke sets it out: since this is offered as a ground for refusing worship, the sense must be that one who has the spirit of prophecy is no higher than one who has the testimony of Christ to preach him among the Gentiles, the commission being equal to the gift. Ellicott identifies the two — the apostle's work was the testimony of Jesus, and the Spirit of prophecy that moved the angel was that same testimony, so one work and one worship belong to both. Robertson puts it that possession of the prophetic spirit shows itself in witness to Jesus, and Wesley that the angel serves as a fellow-servant testifying of the Lord Jesus by the Spirit that inspired the prophets of old.
11:
Gill is careful about what this vision is not: not the first seal, which respects the first times of the Gospel where this respects the last; not the war in heaven with the dragon, which issued in the downfall of Paganism where this will issue in the downfall of the Papacy; not the personal coming to judgment, which belongs to the next chapter. It is the battle at Armageddon, prepared for by the sixth vial. Henry places it in the same sequence, the marriage no sooner solemnised by the conversion of the Jews than the husband of the church is called out on a new expedition; Barnes takes it for the final victory over the beast and false prophet, Clarke for the triumph after the destruction of the enemies.

Whether this rider is the rider of the first seal divides two of them. Ellicott treats it as the same hope renewed: the vision of a conquering Christ had been first a hope and then a despair as age after age interposed its obstacles, and returns now with added splendour, the rider's name dispelling all fear. Robertson grants that the white horse is the emblem of victory in both places and then says the riders are very different. On the name they divide the sense: Ellicott finds in Faithful and True both fidelity to promises and the power to satisfy every desire he has awakened; Wesley splits the pair — faithful in performing his promises, true in executing his threatenings. Wesley makes the colour military, the white of generals in triumph, set against the meekness of the ass so many disregarded; Henry reads the same white as the equity of the cause and the certainty of success.

The name that no one knows is taken two ways. Barnes denies that it means the name could not be read: no one but Christ could understand its import, which involves a knowledge of the nature of the Deity. Wesley says the same in a line, that as God he is incomprehensible to every creature; Henry, that only this much is known of it, that the Word was God. Clarke makes it literal, referring the phrase to the ineffable name the Jews never attempt to pronounce, reading Adonai in its place, and which they say to a man that no one can pronounce, the true sound having been lost since the captivity. Robertson connects it with the new name promised twice earlier, and notices that the diadems are new — not mere crowns but the royal diadems worn severally by the dragon on his seven heads and by the beast on his ten horns, now worn together by the King of kings.

Whose blood stains the vesture is not settled. Gill offers three possibilities — his own, by which he became the Saviour; the saints' blood, which he comes to avenge; or, as he prefers, the blood of enemies not yet killed, the garment stained before the battle because the victory is certain — adding that the figure may recall the purple a Roman general fought in. Henry allows the first two. Wesley takes it for the blood of enemies already conquered, Clarke that he is just come from slaughter, adding that the description is drawn from the prophet, where the figure is Judas Maccabeus or some other conqueror. Robertson closes both questions: the manuscripts divide between sprinkled and dipped, and he prefers the first because the picture comes from that prophet, where two Greek translators use it, granting that dipped is bolder and has been defended; either way it is the blood of Christ's enemies, prophetically anticipated, not his own blood on Calvary. On the last title Clarke notes that the Targum uses the same phrase for the Word of Jehovah and always means a person by it; Barnes, that the name belongs in the New Testament only to John.
14:
Who the heavenly armies are is answered four ways. Gill rules the angels out from the dress: the fine linen is the righteousness of the saints, and the righteousness of angels and of saints is not the same. Ellicott argues the identical point — some would limit these to angels, but the apparel is conclusive against it. Barnes excludes angels on other grounds, that there would be incongruity in representing them as riding so, and draws a distinction the others do not: these hosts accompany him to witness the victory, not to engage in the work of blood, since the prophet has him treading the winepress alone. Clarke will have both, angels and saints together, over whom Christ is Captain; Robertson leans the other way, citing the war of Michael and his angels.

The sword out of the mouth changes meaning between the chapters, or does not. Barnes says that in the opening vision it was an emblem of his words penetrating men's hearts, and here an emblem of destruction wrought on his foes. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from what the text leaves out: the epithet two-edged is dropped, and the omission is not without significance, the sword being wielded now for one work only — the word Christ spoke will judge men at the last day, its power shown in miniature when the band that came to take him fell back. Clarke holds to the earlier sense, taking it for the word of the Gospel by which his enemies are confounded and his friends comforted. Robertson makes it a figure for judicial condemnation; Gill takes it for the word of God or the sentence given according to it, and notes that several versions read twoedged here as well.

The rod of iron sets Cyril against everyone else. Ellicott and Robertson both notice that the verb is to shepherd, so the rule is a shepherd's with an iron staff, and Wesley reads it as the alternative to a golden sceptre for those who will not submit — then applies it to history, holding that the nations felt that rod when the heathen Romans groaned under plagues after persecuting the Christians, and again when other heathen were broken by men bearing the Christian name; and though he calls the cruelty of the Spaniards in America detestable, he holds God executed a righteous judgment by it. Cyril refers the rod of iron not to Christ's rule at all but to the kingdom of the Romans, which he says he has already shown to be meant by it, and brings in Daniel's stone cut without hands to say what overthrows it.

The name on the vesture and the thigh draws four voices to the same ancient custom, two of them to the same authority. Gill explains it from the practice of great persons having their names woven into their garments, sometimes in gold, and offers two accounts of the thigh — the part of the garment covering it, or the sword girt upon it. Barnes pictures the military cloak open and flowing so the name is conspicuous whether wrapped close or loose, and reports Grotius's view that it stood on the sword-hilt at the thigh; nothing in the original, he adds, marks the title out in capitals. Clarke gathers the fullest evidence: it was an ancient custom to adorn images of deities, princes and victors with inscriptions expressing their character, images survive with the inscription on the garment or on a thigh, and Grotius took the word for the imperial robe. Wesley says the same about the eastern practice of affixing titles to garments. Robertson notes that the title has been used before of the Lamb, in reverse order; and Cyril, charging his hearers to keep the deposit of faith unspotted until the appearing, reaches the same words by way of the apostle's charge to Timothy rather than by this vision.
17:
Gill clears the ground before identifying the angel in the sun. It is not the angel of the fourth vial, who poured it on the sun in another sense and so could not stand in it; not the archangel of the last trumpet, since the dead do not yet rise nor has the judgment come; not one of the ministering spirits; and not Christ, since it is the great God to whose supper this angel invites. What remains, he says, is a minister of the Gospel, or rather a whole order of them — standing in the sun as the woman was clothed with it, to signify how conspicuous the preachers will then be, her teachers no longer removed into corners, and how clearly they will see the doctrines of the Gospel when they see eye to eye.

The others take the figure as it stands. Barnes remarks that a great number of angels appear in this book, each on a new errand, and then pauses over the artistry of the sentence: the description is as simple as it can be and as sublime, the fewest possible words used and the image still distinct — a heavenly being standing in the blaze of the brightest orb we are permitted to see, unconsumed and himself bright enough to be seen amid that splendour. Why the angel is placed in the sun, Barnes says, is not stated, and nothing more is intended than grandeur. Robertson supplies exactly the reason Barnes declines to look for, quoting Beckwith that it is where all the birds of prey would behold him. Clarke reads the position as luminosity, every part of the angel emitting rays, and observes that Milton took his Uriel, the angel of the sun, from this representation, quoting the lines.

On the summons itself the notes converge on one prophet. Robertson says the metaphor is drawn from Ezekiel and calls the scene a sacrificial feast spread on God's table for all the vultures of the sky, adding the question whether this battle is the same as the one at Har-Magedon and the later one of Gog and Magog. Wesley refers the figure to the same prophet and takes it as a measure of the vastness of the coming slaughter, a great feast which the vengeance of God will soon provide. Clarke sets beside it a rabbinic tradition that when God executes vengeance for Israel he will feed all the beasts of the earth for twelve months with their flesh and all the fowls for seven years, remarking that beasts and birds of prey are in fact known to frequent fields of battle. Barnes notes only that the cry was loud enough for all the fowls of heaven to hear.

What it means to eat the flesh of kings divides Gill from the rest completely. He reads it politically: the kings are either the antichristian states that drank of Rome's wine or the pagan kings drawn in by the pope and the Turk, and eating their flesh means that on their defeat the Christian princes will seize and possess their kingdoms and dominions. The others keep the carnage literal and differ only in how they fill it in. Barnes goes through the ranks one by one, glossing the Greek word for the second class as commanders of a thousand — colonel, he says, would better convey the idea — taking the third for the robust soldiery, and observing that freemen and slaves are often mingled in the same army, as they were in the American Revolution. Robertson renders the noun as pieces of flesh and closes the list with the remark that war is no respecter of persons. Clarke sums it in a line: there shall be a universal destruction, the kings, the generals, the captains and all their host.
19:
What the beast is gets a different answer from nearly everyone. Gill excludes the devil, since after this he is bound a thousand years, and the Roman pagan empire, destroyed long ago under the sixth seal, and settles on the antichristian civil powers — chiefly the western antichrist, though he lets in the eastern and the Mahometan powers as well. Barnes reads the same alliance, the Roman, the Pagan and the Mohammedan powers roused to make common cause against the true religion. Clarke decodes the three figures separately and exactly: the beast is the Latin empire, the image of the beast the popes of Rome, and the false prophet the papal clergy. Wesley takes the kings for the ten of the earlier chapter, who have now drawn in the rest, Popish, Mahometan or pagan, and adds that all beings, good and evil, visible and invisible, will be concerned in this contest. Robertson looks the other way, noting that the beast had led a league of ten kings against Babylon while intending all along to fight the Lamb, and reporting the view that the false prophet is the priesthood of the imperial cult, which used every imposture to beguile men into worshipping the beast. Cyril applies the gathering against the Lord and his Anointed not to any of this but to the Jews of his own day, who confess one God and deny that he is the Father of Christ, and so, he says, rage and gather themselves together still.

That the two leaders are taken alive while their hosts are killed is noticed by all and explained differently. Barnes finds a propriety in it: the authors of the war are reserved for a severer punishment than death on the field, while their deceived followers are simply cut down. Wesley takes alive at its word and builds a symmetry on it — here is the last of the beast, gone alive into hell after repeated strokes of omnipotence; two went alive into heaven, and perhaps two go alive into hell, so that as Enoch and Elijah may have entered glory at once without waiting in paradise, these two plunge at once into the extremest torment without being reserved in chains of darkness until the judgment of the great day. Clarke will not have the word literally at all: they were discomfited when alive, in the zenith of their power, and so destroyed with an utter destruction. Robertson observes that those merely caught up in the emperor-worship were not thrown into the lake along with the two.

The sword that kills the rest is read as a word rather than a weapon. Barnes says they were cut down by a word, falling as he spoke, and draws the inference that the effect may be a moral one — these powers subdued by the word of the Son of God rather than by slaughter. Clarke says the same in a line, that the sword of him who sat on the horse is his word, the unadulterated Gospel. Gill keeps the list concrete, the remains of Papists, Pagans and Mahometans in every part of the world; Robertson notes only that the birds were filled as they had been invited to be.

Wesley closes with an observation about the writing itself that none of the others make. The chapter is a magnificent description of the overthrow, and it has one exquisite beauty: after the two opposing armies have been exhibited and all the apparatus of a battle set out, the account of the victory follows immediately, without one word of an engagement or of fighting. He calls this the most exact propriety, since there can be no struggle between omnipotence and the power of all creation united against it — and holds that every description must have fallen short of that admirable silence.
